summary: The viewer draws the atom positions a structure file gives (PDB, mmCIF, SDF/MOL or XYZ), and measures distances and angles between atom centers from those positions. The readers are checked against known values: atom counts, the same structure read from two formats, crambin's peptide bonds, backbone angles and disulfide bridges, and caffeine's C=O bonds. The cartoon, the surface and the colors are drawings of that data; where they simplify, it is said below.

claims.claim: Atoms are where the file puts them: the first model, the first alternate location, the same positions whether the structure comes as PDB or mmCIF.
claims.how: The PDB reader takes the fixed columns of ATOM and HETATM records; the mmCIF reader takes the _atom_site table. Crambin (1CRN) read both ways gives the same 327 atoms, elements, positions and B-factors.

sources.title: Atomic Coordinate Entry Format Version 3.3, Coordinate Section
sources.says: ATOM record, columns 31–38: orthogonal coordinates for X in Angstroms (Y and Z follow, then occupancy and temperature factor).

sources.title: 1CRN: Water structure of a hydrophobic protein at atomic resolution
sources.says: Crambin, 46 residues, X-ray diffraction at 1.5 Å.

claims.claim: Distances are in ångströms and angles in degrees, between atom centers; crambin's peptide bonds measure 1.33 Å and its N–CA–C angles 111°, as standard protein geometry says.
claims.how: A distance is the straight line between two atoms' positions; an angle is taken at the middle atom from the two directions to the others. Across crambin's 45 peptide bonds the mean C–N length is within 0.01 Å of 1.329 Å, and the mean N–CA–C angle within 1° of 111.2°.

sources.title: PROCHECK Operating Manual, Appendix A: Engh & Huber parameters
sources.says: Main-chain bond lengths and bond angles as observed in small molecules (Engh & Huber, 1991): C–N 1.329 Å (σ 0.014); N–Cα–C 111.2° (σ 2.8).

claims.note: The measured values are the experiment's model; the toy adds no uncertainty to them.

claims.claim: Bonds come from the file where it lists them, and otherwise from distances with standard covalent radii.
claims.how: SDF/MOL bond blocks and PDB CONECT records are read as given. Otherwise two atoms are bonded when they are closer than the sum of their covalent radii (Cordero et al. 2008) plus 0.45 Å, and a hydrogen keeps only its nearest partner. In crambin this finds exactly its three disulfide bridges (Cys 3–40, 4–32 and 16–26), each about 2.04 Å; caffeine read as XYZ gets the same 25 bonds its SDF lists.

sources.title: Covalent radius
sources.says: Cites B. Cordero et al., "Covalent radii revisited", Dalton Trans. (21), 2832–2838 (2008), for single-bond covalent radii.

sources.title: Disulfide
sources.says: The disulfide bond is about 2.05 Å in length.

claims.note: Distance rules can miss unusual bonds or join atoms that are only crowded; the Toy tab says which way the bonds were found.

claims.claim: Double bonds from an SDF file are drawn as two sticks; caffeine's two C=O bonds are 1.22 Å long.
claims.how: The bond order is read from the file's bond block; caffeine's ideal coordinates from the PDB's Chemical Component Dictionary give C=O bonds of 1.216 and 1.218 Å.

sources.title: Carbonyl group
sources.says: For organic compounds, the length of the C–O bond does not vary widely from 120 picometers.

sources.title: CFF, caffeine
sources.publisher: RCSB Protein Data Bank (Chemical Component Dictionary)
sources.says: Caffeine, C8 H10 N4 O2, with ideal coordinates.

claims.claim: Helices and strands come from the file's records; when a file has none they are worked out from backbone hydrogen bonds, and the toy says so.
claims.how: HELIX and SHEET records (PDB) or _struct_conf and _struct_sheet_range (mmCIF) mark the residues. Without them, a simplified DSSP finds backbone hydrogen bonds with Kabsch and Sander's electrostatic energy (below -0.5 kcal/mol) and builds helices from turns and strands from bridges, up to 3,000 amino acids. For crambin the file gives helices 7–19 and 23–30 and strands 1–4 and 32–35; with the records removed, the worked-out version agrees on more than three quarters of the residues.

sources.title: DSSP (algorithm)
sources.says: A hydrogen bond is identified if E = 0.084 {1/rON + 1/rCH − 1/rOH − 1/rCN} · 332 kcal/mol is less than −0.5 kcal/mol.

claims.note: The worked-out version is a simplified DSSP (no 3-10 or pi helix types of their own, no turns or bends), labeled as inferred.

claims.claim: Space-filling atoms are drawn at their van der Waals radii (Bondi), in the familiar CPK colors.
claims.how: Radii from Bondi (1964): H 1.20, C 1.70, N 1.55, O 1.52, S 1.80 Å and so on; Mantina et al. (2009) for main-group elements Bondi left out; 2.0 Å for elements with neither (the toy says so). Colors are Jmol's CPK colors, carbon a little lighter for the dark stage.

sources.title: Van der Waals radius
sources.says: Hydrogen 1.2, carbon 1.7, nitrogen 1.55, oxygen 1.52, sulfur 1.8 Å: van der Waals radii taken from Bondi's compilation (1964).

sources.title: CPK coloring
sources.says: Column J is the color scheme used by the molecular visualizer Jmol.

claims.note: Ball-and-stick balls are a quarter of the van der Waals radius, a drawing convention.

claims.claim: The molecular surface is close to the surface a water molecule can touch, but smoothed.
claims.how: Each heavy atom adds exp(B(1 − d²/R²)) with R its van der Waals radius, so a lone atom's surface lies exactly at R; the surface is drawn where the sum reaches 1, sampled on a grid. Between crowded atoms the sum fills the gaps, as the solvent-excluded surface of a 1.4 Å probe does, but deep crevices come out shallower.

sources.title: Accessible surface area
sources.says: The accessible surface is created by tracing the center of the probe sphere as it rolls along the van der Waals surface; the typical probe radius is 1.4 Å.

claims.note: Not a rolled-probe surface: an approximation, said in the Toy tab.

simplified: The cartoon is a drawing: a ribbon through the CA atoms (phosphates for DNA and RNA) with set widths, not a measured shape.
The surface is a blobby Gaussian surface over the heavy atoms, close to the solvent-excluded surface but smoother.
Big structures are drawn with fewer splats: one Gaussian per atom, and past the budget only the atoms on the outside (said in the Toy tab).
Only the first model and the first alternate location of each residue are shown.
A flat 2D drawing opened as MOL or SDF gets a 3D shape built by Splashery's embedder; its lengths and angles are estimates, and the toy says so.
